youtube.title: The Mississippi vs Latin America: A River Map and a $72,000 Gap
youtube.description:
One river system drains 41 percent of the lower 48 United States and sends its barges to a single door at New Orleans. South America has the largest river on Earth and a basin the same size as the Mississippi's, yet it took a very different path. In 1700, by Angus Maddison's estimates, Mexico was richer than the colonies that became the US. So did the map decide who got rich, or did people?

On the map: the Mississippi's 1,800 navigable miles, Spain's silver roads from Potosí to Seville, the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, the borders that split the Río de la Plata basin, the Nobel-winning case that rules matter more than rivers, and what could change the map next, from Old River, Louisiana to the new port at Chancay, Peru.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: Which shapes a country's wealth more: its rivers or its rules? 👇

sources.claim: The Mississippi river system drains 41 percent of the lower 48 states
sources.source: US EPA, Mississippi River/Gulf of Mexico Hypoxia Task Force, 'The Mississippi/Atchafalaya River Basin' (accessed 2024)

sources.claim: The basin covers about 1.2 million square miles, 31 states and two Canadian provinces; fourth largest watershed on Earth
sources.source: US National Park Service, Mississippi National River and Recreation Area, 'Mississippi River Facts'

sources.claim: Barges work about 1,800 river miles of the main stem from Minneapolis to the Gulf
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers: Upper Mississippi 9-Foot Channel Project (St. Paul District) and Lower Mississippi, 953.8 miles Cairo to Head of Passes (Mississippi Valley Division)

sources.claim: The Ohio adds 981 navigable miles from Pittsburgh
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, Great Lakes and Ohio River Division, Ohio River navigation

sources.claim: The Missouri has a 735-mile navigation channel from Sioux City, Iowa
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, Northwestern Division, Missouri River Bank Stabilization and Navigation Project

sources.claim: The Mississippi, Ohio and Missouri routes alone, about 3,500 miles, all lead to the lower river between Baton Rouge and the Gulf
sources.source: Sum of the US Army Corps of Engineers figures above: about 1,800 + 981 + 735 miles; all three join the main stem above Baton Rouge

sources.claim: The United States is the world's largest corn producer
sources.source: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, Grain: World Markets and Trade, 2024

sources.claim: St. Louis stands less than 150 metres above sea level, over 1,000 river miles from the sea
sources.source: USGS Geographic Names Information System (St. Louis, about 142 m); USACE river miles (St. Louis about 180 miles above the Ohio confluence, plus 953.8 to Head of Passes)

sources.claim: A gallon of fuel moves a ton of cargo 647 miles by barge, 477 by rail and 145 by truck
sources.source: Texas A&M Transportation Institute, 'A Modal Comparison of Domestic Freight Transportation Effects on the General Public', 2017

sources.claim: One 15-barge tow carries as much as about 1,050 semi trucks
sources.source: Iowa Department of Transportation, 'Barge, rail and truck cargo capacity comparison', citing Texas A&M Transportation Institute

sources.claim: About 12,000 miles of commercial inland waterways maintained by the Army Corps
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, Inland Waterways Users Board annual report, 2023

sources.claim: Ocean ships sail about 230 river miles up to Baton Rouge
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, New Orleans District, Mississippi River Ship Channel, Gulf to Baton Rouge

sources.claim: About six in ten US grain exports leave from the Mississippi Gulf ports
sources.source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, 'The Importance of Inland Waterways to U.S. Agriculture', 2019

sources.claim: Stratfor wrote in 2011 that the Greater Mississippi basin has more navigable waterways than the rest of the world combined
sources.source: Stratfor, 'The Geopolitics of the United States, Part 1', 2011

sources.claim: China counts about 128,000 km of navigable inland waterways
sources.source: Ministry of Transport of the People's Republic of China, Statistical Bulletin on Transport Industry Development, 2023

sources.claim: The Amazon carries about one fifth of the fresh water rivers deliver to the oceans
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Amazon River'

sources.claim: Ocean ships reach Iquitos, about 3,700 km upriver; Iquitos has no road link to Lima
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Amazon River' and 'Iquitos'

sources.claim: The Río de la Plata basin covers about 3.1 million square kilometres across Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Río de la Plata'

sources.claim: Mexico City 2,240 m, Bogotá 2,640 m, Quito 2,850 m
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica city entries

sources.claim: São Paulo stands about 760 metres up, about 65 km from Santos, behind the Serra do Mar
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'São Paulo' and 'Santos'

sources.claim: Mexico about $568 per person in 1700 vs $527 in the future US; 1820: US $1,257, Mexico $759; 1913: US $5,301, Argentina $3,797, Mexico $1,732 (1990 international dollars, estimates)
sources.source: Angus Maddison, 'The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective', OECD, 2001

sources.claim: Potosí lies over 4,000 metres up; its silver went by mule to Arica, by sea to Callao, across Panama and on to Spain
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Potosí'; Peter Bakewell, 'Miners of the Red Mountain', 1984

sources.claim: The Casa de Contratación in Seville was set up in 1503
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Casa de Contratación'

sources.claim: Buenos Aires was kept off legal trade routes for most of the colonial era; viceroyalty capital in 1776; trade rules loosened in 1778
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata' and 'Buenos Aires'

sources.claim: The 1795 Pinckney Treaty gave Americans navigation and the right of deposit at New Orleans
sources.source: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Pinckney's Treaty, 1795'

sources.claim: In 1800 Spain secretly agreed to pass Louisiana back to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso; transfer took effect 1802-03); Spain suspended the right of deposit in October 1802
sources.source: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, 'Louisiana Purchase, 1803'

sources.claim: Jefferson: 'There is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans...'
sources.source: Thomas Jefferson to Robert R. Livingston, 18 April 1802, Founders Online, US National Archives

sources.claim: Louisiana bought for $15 million, about 828,000 square miles, roughly doubling the country; New Orleans and the river's mouth passed to the US, while the east bank above the Isle of Orleans stayed Spanish until 1810-1812
sources.source: US National Archives, 'Louisiana Purchase Treaty (1803)'; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'West Florida Controversy'

sources.claim: In 1811 the first steamboat on these rivers left Pittsburgh for New Orleans; practical upstream steamboating followed within a few years (Enterprise, 1815)
sources.source: National Park Service; Smithsonian National Museum of American History, 'The New Orleans' steamboat; Louis C. Hunter, 'Steamboats on the Western Rivers', 1949

sources.claim: Erie Canal opened 1825; Illinois and Michigan Canal joined Lake Michigan to the Mississippi system in 1848
sources.source: New York State Canal Corporation; National Park Service, Illinois and Michigan Canal National Heritage Corridor

sources.claim: Spanish America won independence between 1810 and the mid-1820s; Gran Colombia 1819-1831, splitting into Venezuela, Ecuador and New Granada (which included Panama); Federal Republic of Central America 1823-1841
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Latin American wars of independence', 'Gran Colombia', 'United Provinces of Central America'

sources.claim: Paraguay fought Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay from 1864 to 1870; causes debated, river access among them
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Paraguayan War'

sources.claim: Geography camp: Peter Zeihan (2014), Tim Marshall (2015)
sources.source: Peter Zeihan, 'The Accidental Superpower', 2014; Tim Marshall, 'Prisoners of Geography', 2015

sources.claim: 2024 economics Nobel to Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson 'for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity'
sources.source: NobelPrize.org, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announcement, 14 October 2024

sources.claim: Why Nations Fail opens in Nogales, split by the US-Mexico border
sources.source: Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, 'Why Nations Fail', 2012, chapter 1

sources.claim: Colonies richest around 1500 tend to be poorer today
sources.source: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, 'Reversal of Fortune', Quarterly Journal of Economics 117(4), 2002

sources.claim: Soils and crops shaped the Americas through inequality: sugar and plantation colonies concentrated land in few hands, wheat and family-farm colonies spread it among many
sources.source: Stanley Engerman and Kenneth Sokoloff, 'Factor Endowments, Institutions, and Differential Paths of Growth Among New World Economies', in Haber (ed.), 'How Latin America Fell Behind', 1997

sources.claim: The institutions camp cites Argentina as a case where institutions, not resources, held growth back
sources.source: Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, 'Why Nations Fail', 2012

sources.claim: Argentina fell behind across the twentieth century
sources.source: Maddison Project Database, 2023 release

sources.claim: Brazil is the world's largest soybean exporter
sources.source: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, Oilseeds: World Markets and Trade, 2024

sources.claim: Trucks drive about 2,000 km from Sorriso to Santos; soy also moves north via the Tapajós to ports near the Amazon mouth
sources.source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Brazil Soybean Transportation report, 2024

sources.claim: Paraguay's shipowners say it runs the world's third largest barge fleet
sources.source: Reuters, reporting on low water on the Paraná, 2021, citing Paraguay's river shipowners' association (CAFyM)

sources.claim: The Paraná-Paraguay waterway runs about 3,442 km from Cáceres to Nueva Palmira
sources.source: Comité Intergubernamental de la Hidrovía Paraguay-Paraná (CIH)

sources.claim: Chancay port opened 14 November 2024; COSCO holds 60 percent, Volcan 40; first phase about $1.3 billion
sources.source: Reuters, 14 November 2024

sources.claim: Peru's government calls Chancay a regional hub; US officials have voiced concern about Chinese control of strategic ports
sources.source: Reuters, November 2024

sources.claim: Some shippers and officials have pointed to Chancay as a route to Asia that avoids the Panama Canal
sources.source: Reuters, November 2024, reporting on Chancay's opening and South American exporters' plans to ship to Asia through it

sources.claim: US GDP per person about $82,800; Latin America and the Caribbean a little over $10,000 (2023); a gap of about $72,000 per person
sources.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, GDP per capita (current US$), 2023; gap computed from these two figures

sources.claim: Record low on the Mississippi at Memphis, October 2022
sources.source: National Weather Service, Memphis, October 2022

sources.claim: Record spot barge rates at St. Louis in October 2022
sources.source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Grain Transportation Report, October 2022

sources.claim: 29 locks and dams on the Upper Mississippi, mostly built in the 1930s, many past their 50-year design life
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, Navigation and Ecosystem Sustainability Program (NESP)

sources.claim: Inland waterways graded D+
sources.source: American Society of Civil Engineers, 2021 Report Card for America's Infrastructure

sources.claim: Engineers have long warned of the Mississippi shifting into the Atchafalaya at Old River; the Atchafalaya reaches the Gulf in about 140 miles vs roughly 300 on the Mississippi's path; a breakthrough could leave Baton Rouge and New Orleans on a saltwater channel
sources.source: John McPhee, 'The Control of Nature', 1989; US Army Corps of Engineers, New Orleans District

sources.claim: Old River Control Structure in place since 1963, passing about 30 percent of the flow to the Atchafalaya
sources.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, New Orleans District, Old River Control Complex

sources.claim: Paraná dredging concession held since 1995 expired in 2021; Argentina has been trying to award a new one since
sources.source: Reuters, April 2021 and 2025

sources.claim: Panama Canal daily transits cut to about 24 from roughly 36 in late 2023 due to drought
sources.source: Panama Canal Authority, advisories to shipping, November 2023

sources.claim: Mexico became the largest US trading partner in 2023, about $798 billion in goods
sources.source: US Census Bureau, US International Trade in Goods and Services, February 2024

sources.claim: Singapore, at the tip of the Malacca Strait, founded as a British trading post in 1819, now has higher output per person than the UK
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Singapore'; World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2023
